q: The genetic material of a virus is:
o: Either DNA or RNA, but never both
x: A virus carries only one kind of nucleic acid: DNA or RNA, never both. It may be single- or double-stranded. This is one of the main ways viruses are classified.

q: The protein coat (capsid) of a virus is built from repeating subunits called:
x: The capsid is made of many protein subunits called capsomeres. Nucleosomes are DNA–histone units in eukaryotic chromosomes. Peplomers are the glycoprotein spikes on a viral envelope, not the capsid.

q: Which virus has a helical (rod-shaped) capsid?
x: Tobacco mosaic virus (TMV) is the classic helical virus: its capsomeres wind around the RNA to form a rod. Adenovirus and poliovirus are polyhedral (icosahedral), and T4 is complex.

q: On the basis of shape, bacteriophage T4 is classified as a:
o: Complex virus with a polyhedral head and a helical tail
x: T4 combines two symmetries: a polyhedral head holding its DNA and a helical tail with a sheath, base plate and tail fibres. Viruses with such mixed structure are called complex viruses.

q: Viruses that infect bacteria are called:
x: Bacteriophages (phages) are viruses whose hosts are bacteria; the name means 'bacteria eaters'. Classifying viruses by host gives plant viruses, animal viruses and bacteriophages.

q: The envelope present around some viruses, such as influenza virus and HIV, is derived from:
o: The membranes of the host cell
x: Enveloped viruses pick up their outer lipid envelope from host cell membranes as they bud out of the cell. Viral glycoproteins are inserted into this envelope.

q: Which of the following is a DNA virus?
x: Hepatitis B virus has DNA as its genetic material. Influenza virus, poliovirus and HIV are all RNA viruses.

q: Which of the following is an RNA virus?
x: Measles virus contains RNA. Herpes simplex virus, adenovirus and the smallpox (pox) virus are DNA viruses.

q: Which virus has double-stranded RNA as its genetic material?
x: Rotavirus, a common cause of diarrhoea in children, has double-stranded RNA. Poliovirus and TMV have a single strand of RNA, and HIV carries two copies of single-stranded RNA.

q: Tobacco mosaic virus was first crystallized in 1935 by:
x: W. M. Stanley crystallized TMV in 1935, showing that a virus can behave like a chemical crystal outside a cell. Ivanowsky (1892) had earlier shown that the tobacco mosaic agent passes through bacteria-proof filters.

q: Viruses are called obligate intracellular parasites because they:
o: Can reproduce only inside a living host cell
Live only in soil and water
x: Viruses have no ribosomes or metabolism of their own. They must use a living host cell's machinery to make copies of themselves, so they can reproduce only inside host cells.

q: The correct sequence of events in the lytic cycle of a bacteriophage is:
x: The phage first attaches to the bacterium, then injects its DNA (penetration). The DNA is copied and phage proteins are made (replication), new phages are put together (assembly), and finally the cell bursts to release them (lysis).

q: In the lysogenic cycle, phage DNA that is inserted into the bacterial chromosome is called a:
x: In lysogeny the phage DNA joins the host chromosome and is copied along with it at each cell division. This integrated phage DNA is called a prophage.

q: A bacteriophage that can enter the lysogenic cycle instead of killing its host straight away is called a:
x: Temperate phages, such as lambda phage, can either kill the cell (lytic cycle) or integrate as a prophage (lysogenic cycle). Virulent phages, like T4, always follow the lytic cycle.

q: During penetration, bacteriophage T4:
o: Enters the bacterium whole by phagocytosis
Injects its protein coat and leaves its DNA outside
Injects its DNA into the bacterium and leaves its protein coat outside
Fuses its lipid envelope with the bacterial cell wall
x: T4 contracts its tail sheath and injects only its DNA through the bacterial wall. The empty protein coat stays outside. T4 has no lipid envelope.

q: The enzyme in the tail of bacteriophage T4 that digests a hole in the bacterial cell wall is:
x: The phage tail carries lysozyme, which breaks down part of the bacterial cell wall so the DNA can be injected. Reverse transcriptase belongs to retroviruses such as HIV.

q: A complete, infectious virus particle outside a host cell is called a:
x: A virion is the complete virus particle: nucleic acid inside a capsid, with an envelope in some viruses. A capsomere is one capsid subunit. Prophage and provirus are viral DNA integrated into a host chromosome.

q: According to classification by host, tobacco mosaic virus is a:
x: TMV infects tobacco and related plants, causing mottled (mosaic) leaves. By host, viruses are grouped as plant viruses, animal viruses and bacteriophages.

q: Which of the following diseases is caused by a virus?
x: Polio is caused by poliovirus. Tuberculosis, cholera and typhoid are bacterial diseases.

q: Antibiotics do not cure viral infections because viruses:
o: Lack the cell walls, ribosomes and metabolism that antibiotics act on
x: Antibiotics work by attacking bacterial structures and processes, such as the cell wall, ribosomes and enzymes. Viruses have none of these of their own, so antibiotics have nothing to act on. Viral infections need antiviral drugs or vaccines.

q: AIDS is caused by:
x: AIDS (acquired immunodeficiency syndrome) is the late stage of infection with HIV, a retrovirus that destroys the immune system.

q: HIV mainly infects and destroys:
x: HIV binds to the CD4 receptor found on helper T cells and destroys them. Helper T cells coordinate both antibody and cell-mediated immunity, so losing them cripples the whole immune system.

q: HIV is called a retrovirus because it:
o: Uses reverse transcriptase to make DNA from its RNA
x: Retroviruses reverse the usual flow of genetic information. The enzyme reverse transcriptase copies their RNA into DNA, which is then inserted into the host cell's DNA.

q: HIV is NOT transmitted by:
o: Shaking hands or sharing food utensils
An infected mother to her baby
x: HIV spreads through sexual contact, blood (transfusion, shared needles and razors), and from mother to baby during pregnancy, birth or breastfeeding. Casual contact, food, utensils and mosquitoes do not spread it.

q: The genetic material of HIV consists of:
x: Each HIV particle carries two identical strands of single-stranded RNA, together with the enzymes reverse transcriptase, integrase and protease.

q: The HIV envelope glycoprotein that binds to the CD4 receptor of a helper T cell is:
x: gp120 on the HIV envelope attaches to CD4 on helper T cells. gp41 then helps the viral envelope fuse with the cell membrane. p24 is a capsid protein, and haemagglutinin belongs to influenza virus.

q: Which group of symptoms is typical of AIDS?
o: Weight loss, persistent fever, swollen lymph nodes and repeated infections
Yellow skin and dark urine only
Paralysis of the limbs from the start
High blood sugar and frequent urination
x: As helper T cells fall, patients develop weight loss, fever, night sweats, chronic diarrhoea, swollen lymph nodes and repeated opportunistic infections.

q: AIDS patients often die of other infections because:
o: HIV causes the body to produce too many antibodies
Loss of helper T cells leaves them unable to fight opportunistic infections
x: HIV itself is rarely the direct cause of death. Once the immune system collapses, infections that a healthy body controls easily become life-threatening. Examples are tuberculosis and Pneumocystis pneumonia.

q: A person recently infected with HIV may test negative on an antibody (ELISA) test because:
o: HIV leaves the blood within a few days
HIV is present only in saliva
Antibodies take several weeks to appear (the window period)
The test detects only bacterial antibodies
x: Antibody tests detect the body's antibodies against HIV, not the virus itself. The immune system takes weeks to make enough antibodies. During this 'window period' the person can test negative but still pass on the virus.

q: The anti-HIV drug zidovudine (AZT) works by:
x: AZT blocks reverse transcriptase, so viral RNA cannot be copied into DNA and the virus cannot multiply. It slows the infection but does not cure it.

q: Which statement about the treatment of HIV infection is correct?
o: Antiretroviral drugs control the virus but do not cure the infection
A single vaccine dose cures AIDS
HIV infection heals on its own within a few weeks
x: Antiretroviral therapy keeps HIV levels low and lets patients live long lives, but the virus remains in the body. There is no cure and no approved HIV vaccine yet, so prevention matters most.

q: Kaposi's sarcoma and Pneumocystis pneumonia are best described as:
o: Opportunistic conditions common in AIDS patients
x: These conditions rarely affect people with healthy immune systems. Their appearance in a patient is a classic sign that HIV has severely weakened immunity, so they are called opportunistic conditions.

q: Which of the following viruses has a lipid envelope around its capsid?
x: Herpes simplex virus is an enveloped virus. Tobacco mosaic virus, poliovirus and adenovirus are naked viruses: their capsid is not covered by an envelope.

q: Most viruses are too small to be seen with a light microscope. They are studied with:
o: A compound light microscope at high power
x: Viruses are measured in nanometres, far below the resolving power of light microscopes. Their structure was seen only after the electron microscope was developed.

q: The word 'virus' comes from a Latin word meaning:
x: 'Virus' is Latin for poison or venom. The name was used for disease-causing agents long before their nature was understood.

q: Which pair correctly matches a virus with its type of genetic material?
x: Poxviruses (such as smallpox virus) have double-stranded DNA. Poliovirus, tobacco mosaic virus and influenza virus all have RNA, not DNA.

q: Which of the following viruses has single-stranded DNA as its genetic material?
x: Parvoviruses are small viruses with single-stranded DNA. Poxviruses, herpesviruses and adenoviruses all have double-stranded DNA.

q: Rabies virus, passed to humans mainly by the bite of an infected dog, chiefly attacks the:
x: Rabies virus travels along nerves to the brain and spinal cord, causing a fatal disease of the nervous system. The parotid glands are the main target of mumps virus.

q: Which crop disease, a serious problem for cotton growers in Pakistan, is caused by a virus?
x: Cotton leaf curl disease is caused by a plant virus spread by whiteflies. Rust of wheat and late blight of potato are fungal diseases, and citrus canker is caused by a bacterium.

q: Which hepatitis viruses are spread mainly through food and water contaminated with faeces?
o: Hepatitis B virus and hepatitis C virus
Hepatitis B virus and hepatitis D virus
Hepatitis C virus and hepatitis D virus
Hepatitis A virus and hepatitis E virus
x: Hepatitis A virus and hepatitis E virus pass by the faecal–oral route through contaminated food and water. Hepatitis B virus, hepatitis C virus and hepatitis D virus spread mainly through blood and body fluids.

q: A prophage can leave the bacterial chromosome and start the lytic cycle. This switch is commonly triggered by:
o: Exposure of the host to ultraviolet light or certain chemicals
Addition of extra nutrients to the growth medium
Binding of antibodies to the bacterium
A rise in the number of host ribosomes
x: Stress such as ultraviolet radiation or certain chemicals can induce the prophage to cut itself out of the host chromosome. It then directs the lytic cycle, making new phages and bursting the cell.

q: In bacteriophage T4, the tail fibres:
o: Attach the phage to specific receptor sites on the bacterial wall
Form the protein coat of the head
x: The tail fibres recognise and bind to specific receptor sites on the bacterial cell wall, which is the attachment step. The DNA is stored in the polyhedral head.

q: A certain virus infects human liver cells but not skin cells. The main reason is that:
o: Liver cells have no immune defences
Only liver cells carry the surface receptors the virus binds to
The virus is destroyed by sunlight on the skin
x: A virus can infect only cells whose surface carries the receptor molecules its attachment proteins fit. This lock-and-key binding decides which hosts and tissues a virus can infect.

q: Which statement about the lysogenic cycle is correct?
o: New phages are assembled and the cell bursts straight away
Phage DNA stays separate from the host chromosome and is destroyed
The host is not killed at once, and the prophage is copied into each daughter cell
It is followed only by virulent phages such as T4
x: In lysogeny the phage DNA joins the host chromosome and is replicated with it, so every daughter cell inherits the prophage. The host survives until the prophage is induced. T4 is virulent and always lytic.

q: Which property of viruses is a characteristic of non-living things?
o: They can be crystallized like chemicals
x: Outside a host cell viruses can be crystallized and show no metabolism, like non-living chemicals. Reproduction, mutation and having nucleic acid are features they share with living things.

q: In classifying viruses by host, most plant viruses are found to contain:
x: Most plant viruses, such as tobacco mosaic virus, are RNA viruses. Most bacteriophages contain DNA, while animal viruses may have either DNA or RNA. No virus has both.

q: Influenza virus spreads from person to person mainly through:
o: Droplets released by coughing and sneezing
x: Influenza is a respiratory infection. The virus is carried in droplets from an infected person's coughs and sneezes and is breathed in by others.

q: Smallpox, a viral disease, was eradicated from the world by:
x: A worldwide vaccination programme eradicated smallpox. Antibiotics have no effect on viruses, and smallpox is not spread by insects or water.

q: Cold sores (fever blisters) around the lips are caused by:
x: Herpes simplex virus, a DNA virus, causes cold sores. It can stay hidden in nerve cells and cause blisters again later.

q: Bacteriophages are added to a lawn of bacteria growing on agar. After some hours, clear patches appear. These patches show:
o: Areas where the phages digested the agar
Colonies of a second kind of bacterium
Bacteria destroyed by phages in the lytic cycle
x: Each clear patch (plaque) is where phages have multiplied and burst the bacteria by the lytic cycle. Lysogenic bacteria survive and keep growing, so they would not leave clear areas.

q: Which human disease is caused by a DNA virus?
x: Chickenpox is caused by the varicella-zoster virus, a DNA virus of the herpes group. Measles, mumps and influenza are caused by RNA viruses.

q: Mumps is a viral disease that causes painful swelling of the:
x: Mumps virus mainly infects the parotid salivary glands below the ears, causing swollen cheeks and jaw. A swollen thyroid is goitre, and an inflamed liver is hepatitis.

q: In the name AIDS, the word 'acquired' means that the condition:
o: Is passed through genes from parents
Is caused by a lack of vitamins in the diet
Develops after infection during life and is not inherited
x: 'Acquired' means the immune deficiency is caught by infection with HIV during a person's life. It is not a genetic (inherited) immune disorder.

q: After reverse transcription, the HIV DNA that becomes part of the host cell's DNA is called a:
x: Viral DNA integrated into an animal cell's chromosome is called a provirus. The term prophage is used for phage DNA integrated into a bacterial chromosome.

q: The HIV enzyme that inserts the newly made viral DNA into the DNA of the helper T cell is:
x: Integrase splices the viral DNA into the host chromosome. Reverse transcriptase acts one step earlier, making DNA from the viral RNA. Lysozyme is a phage enzyme.

q: The correct order of events when HIV infects a helper T cell is:
o: Binding to CD4 → entry → integration → reverse transcription → budding
Binding to CD4 → entry → reverse transcription → integration → budding
Reverse transcription → binding to CD4 → entry → integration → budding
Binding to CD4 → integration → entry → reverse transcription → budding
x: HIV binds CD4 and enters the cell. Its RNA must first be copied into DNA by reverse transcriptase before it can be integrated. The cell then makes viral parts, and new viruses bud out.

q: New HIV particles leave an infected helper T cell by:
o: Bursting the cell wall with lysozyme
Being injected through a tail into another cell
Binary fission of the viral particle
x: HIV particles bud out through the host cell membrane, wrapping themselves in part of it as their envelope. Bursting with lysozyme and tail injection describe bacteriophages.

q: Besides helper T cells, which cells can HIV also infect because they carry CD4 receptors?
x: Macrophages also carry CD4 on their surface, so HIV can infect them and they can act as a reservoir of the virus. Red blood cells, muscle fibres and bone cells are not HIV targets.

q: A hospital wants to stop HIV being passed on through blood transfusion. The most direct measure is to:
o: Give every patient antibiotics before transfusion
Store blood at a lower temperature
Transfuse only blood of the same group
Screen all donated blood for HIV before use
x: Testing donated blood for HIV and discarding infected units prevents transmission. Antibiotics do not act on viruses, and cooling or blood-group matching does not remove HIV.

q: HIV is present in enough amount to cause infection in which of these body fluids?
x: HIV is transmitted by blood, semen, vaginal fluid and breast milk, which is why an infected mother can pass it to her baby by breastfeeding. Sweat, tears and urine do not spread HIV.

q: Which of the following practices carries a risk of HIV transmission?
o: Sharing razors or unsterilised tattoo needles
Swimming in the same pool as an infected person
x: Razors and needles can carry traces of infected blood into another person's body. HIV does not survive in pool water, is not carried by mosquitoes and is not spread by casual contact.

q: A person infected with HIV may look healthy for several years. This is because:
o: The virus is destroyed soon after infection
Helper T cells fall slowly, so symptoms appear only when immunity is badly weakened
HIV infects only nerve cells during this time
The person has become permanently immune to the virus
x: After infection there is a long period without symptoms while HIV slowly destroys helper T cells. During this time the person can still pass on the virus.

q: The progress of HIV infection towards AIDS is followed by measuring the number of which cells in the blood?
x: HIV destroys CD4 helper T cells, so their falling count shows how far the infection has progressed. A very low CD4 count marks the stage of AIDS.

q: HIV infects helper T cells, yet both antibody-mediated and cell-mediated immunity fail. The reason is that helper T cells:
o: Make all the antibodies of the body
Are the only cells that can kill bacteria
Produce the red blood cells that carry oxygen
Are needed to activate both B cells and cytotoxic T cells
x: Helper T cells stimulate B cells to make antibodies and activate cytotoxic T cells. When they are lost, both branches of the immune response weaken. Antibodies themselves are made by plasma cells, not helper T cells.

q: A major reason why no effective HIV vaccine has been made is that HIV:
o: Has no proteins on its surface
Mutates rapidly, so its envelope proteins keep changing
Is too large to be recognised by antibodies
Infects only bacteria in the gut
x: Reverse transcriptase makes many copying errors, so HIV mutates quickly and its surface glycoproteins keep changing. Antibodies raised against one form may not recognise the next.
